claims.claim: The Farmer Giles chronicle fixes its events by the church calendar (St Nicholas' Day, Christmas Eve, 14 January) inside a legendary span 'between Brutus and King Arthur'.

Farmer Giles's pose as a translated manuscript with commentary on its origins and dubious place-name etymology parodies scholarly works including the Prologue to Tolkien's own Lord of the Rings, mocking the medieval appeal to authority.
claims.quote: parody of scholarly works, including the prologue

claims.claim: The tale's narrator was 'Daddy' in the oral original, became 'the family jester', and took on a formal scholarly tone when the story was enlarged by half for an academic essay club in 1938.
claims.source: Hammond & Scull, 'Farmer Giles of Ham' (Tolkien Estate)

claims.claim: By its 1949 publication the children's tale had acquired the mock-scholarly foreword, so the record register was a deliberate late addition rather than the story's native voice.
claims.source: Philip Irving Mitchell, 'Farmer Giles of Ham: Comedy in Faërie?' (DBU)

claims.claim: Shippey identifies the Middle Kingdom of Farmer Giles with early Mercia, its capital possibly Tamworth, so the record's geography is a calque on real English history.
Kullmann finds the Prologue imitates the non-fictional prose of nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century ethnography, while the Note on the Shire Records mimics works of historiography.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Editorial framing of The Lord of the Rings' (citing Kullmann & Siepmann 2021, pp. 46–47)
claims.quote: non-fictional prose of nineteenth- and early twentieth-century ethnography

claims.claim: 'Concerning Hobbits' places the text in the stylistic mode of nineteenth-century English antiquarianism, like a treatise on regional folklore, signalling to the reader a departure from modern novelistic conventions.
claims.quote: a certain strain of nineteenth-century English antiquarianism

claims.claim: Halbrooks argues Tolkien's greatest strength is that he very carefully adjusts his prose style and even his generic conventions according to the narrative circumstances.
claims.quote: he very carefully adjusts his prose style

claims.claim: The Shire is 'calqued' on England element by element: three founding tribes, a forgotten origin, founding brothers with horse-names, and a 272-year peace between battles matching the 270 years since Sedgemoor.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'

claims.claim: Organisationally the Shire, with its mayors, musters, moots and Shirriffs, is an old-fashioned and idealised England.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'

claims.claim: Modern names are perceived as labels isomorphic with reality, so a dense name-stock weighs fantasy down with repeated implicit assurances that the things labelled exist; this is strongest in the Shire's map, account and history.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: repeated implicit assurances of the existence of the things

claims.claim: Speakers in The Lord of the Rings have a strong tendency to talk like historical maps, reeling off names and river courses, a habit shared by Aragorn, Celeborn, Gimli, Gandalf and Meriadoc.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth, ch. 4 'A Cartographic Plot'
claims.quote: talk like maps, historical ones at that

claims.claim: The Prologue says 'pipe-weed' rather than tobacco because the imported word would sound wrong, and hedges its botany with a Latin binomial instead.
claims.source: Tom Shippey, The Road to Middle-earth

claims.claim: The Note on the Shire Records credits Meriadoc with a Herblore of the Shire, a Reckoning of Years comparing calendars, and a treatise on Old Words and Names, so the record cites fictional reference works by title.
claims.source: Giuseppe Pezzini, 'The authors of Middle Earth' (J. Inklings Studies 2018), quoting the Note
claims.quote: Old Words and Names in the Shire

claims.claim: 'Concerning Pipe-weed' began as a lengthy speech by Merry in a draft of 'The Road to Isengard' that was removed and reworked into the Prologue, so dialogue was converted into record.
claims.source: Tolkien Gateway, 'Prologue (The Lord of the Rings)'
claims.quote: a lengthy speech of Merry about pipe-weed

verdicts.trueWording: sets it between Brutus settling the lands and King Arthur
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (200, live). Claim carries no quote field. Page has all three dates in the narrative: 'He was supposed to set out upon St. Nicholas' Day', 'carried this into the hall on Christmas Eve', and the dragon's oath 'to return on January the fourteenth'. The claim's internal quoted span 'between Brutus and King Arthur' is NOT verbatim; footnote 4 reads 'sets it sometime between the time that Brutus settled the lands and King Arthur'. 'Church calendar' is the claimant's gloss (two of the three dates are feast days; 14 January is not).

verdicts.trueWording: parody of scholarly works, including the prologue to Tolkien's own The Lord of the Rings
verdicts.note: Live URL returned HTTP 403 with a browser UA; recovered via Wayback raw capture 20251207034747id_. Quote verbatim under the 'Parodic Commentary' subheading of Style and Technique. Every limb present: 'poses as a translation of an ancient manuscript, complete with amusing commentary on its origins and dubious etymology of place names' and 'humorously critiques the appeal to "authority" often seen in medieval manuscripts'.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that the narrator took on a formal scholarly tone at the 1938 enlargement — the page dates the mock-scholarly voice to the 1949 revision instead
verdicts.trueWording: For this larger, more academic audience, he added many proper names, jokes, and allusions
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (200, live). Quote 'the family jester' is verbatim: 'In the second version of the story, the narrator is "the family jester"'. Supported: narrated by 'Daddy' in the first version; 'enlarging it by some fifty per cent' in January 1938 for the Lovelace Society, 'an undergraduate essay club at Oxford's Worcester College'. NOT supported: any narratorial shift to scholarly tone at that 1938 stage — the page says the 1938 additions were 'proper names, jokes, and allusions', and places the apparatus later: 'Tolkien again revised the text, and added a mock foreword' before the 1949 publication. Second minor slip: 'Daddy' narrates the first written version, not the oral original.

verdicts.trueWording: by its publication in 1949, it had acquired the mock-scholarly forward
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (200, live). Quote verbatim including the page's own misspelling 'forward'. 'Children's tale' limb supported by 'it originated in the 1920's as a tale for Tolkien's children'; the late-addition inference is licensed by the page's own chronology (1920s children's tale, expanded 1938 for the Lovelace Society, foreword by 1949).

verdicts.trueWording: the Middle Kingdom is based on early Mercia ... could well be Tamworth
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext fetched via Special:Export (200). Quote 'based on early Mercia' verbatim; Tamworth limb verbatim ('could well be Tamworth, once Mercia's capital'), cited to Shippey 2005 p. 111. Three locator/wording flags, none of them a claim limb: the sentence sits in section 'Quasi-realistic historical setting', NOT the '§ Quasi-realistic geographical setting' the claim names; the article says Shippey 'suggests', not 'identifies'; and the word 'calque' appears zero times in the article (it is Shippey's term for the Shire, imported by the claimant). The geography-on-real-England substance is separately supported by the geographical-setting section (Oakley, Otmoor, Rollright Stones, Thame, Worminghall).

verdicts.trueWording: prologue obviously imitates the non-fictional prose of ... ethnography; Notes on Shire Records imitate works of historiography
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext fetched via Special:Export (200). Quote verbatim in section 'Multiple elements'; the historiography limb is verbatim too. Citation flag: the article attributes this to Kullmann 2009 (Nordic Journal of English Studies 8.2), pp. 46-47 — 'Siepmann' does not occur anywhere in the article, so the claim's source field 'Kullmann & Siepmann 2021' is wrong even though the page numbers match. Also the article writes 'Notes on Shire Records'; Tolkien's title is 'Note on the Shire Records'.

verdicts.trueWording: the stylistic mode of a certain strain of nineteenth-century English antiquarianism
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (200, live); datePublished 2024-03-13 confirms the citation. Quote verbatim. Regional-folklore limb supported by the page's invented titles ('Concerning Traditional Bee-Keeping Techniques in Kent...', 'Concerning Aphorisms in the North Yorkshire Dialect'); the departure-from-the-novel limb is near-verbatim: 'The Prologue lets readers know right away that they are not about to begin a modern novel'.

verdicts.trueWording: he very carefully adjusts his prose style, and even his generic conventions and assumptions, according to the narrative circumstances
verdicts.note: Raw page fetched (200, live). Quote verbatim. 'Greatest strength' is the claimant's superlative, not the page's phrase, but the page supports it twice over: prose style is 'where he usually succeeds where most of his imitators fail miserably', and 'This flexibility of voice and tone is the single most important factor in the continued success of the book over the past seven decades.'

verdicts.trueWording: weighing it down ... with repeated implicit assurances of the existence of the things they label
verdicts.note: Same raw book text. Quote verbatim. Isomorphism limb verbatim: 'In the modern world we take them as labels ... To use a pompous phrase, they are "isomorphic with reality"'. Shire limb verbatim: 'Tolkien's new equation of fantasy with reality comes over most strongly in his map, account and history of "the Shire"'. Sits between the p. 92 and p. 93 running heads, matching the citation.

verdicts.trueWording: characters ... have a strong tendency to talk like maps, historical ones at that
verdicts.note: Same raw book text. Quote verbatim. Aragorn (Limlight/Riddermark) and Celeborn (tracing Anduin to Tol Brandir, Rauros, Nindalf, Entwash) are the worked examples; 'the habit is shared by Gimli, Gandalf, Fangorn, even Meriadoc' covers the rest — the claim omits Fangorn but adds nobody. 'Reeling off names' matches 'The flow of knowledge, and of names, seems irrepressible'. Precedes the p. 92 running head, so p. 91 as cited.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'a Latin binomial' — the page shows only the genus name, Tolkien's hedge 'a variety probably of Nicotiana', which is a uninomial, not a binomial
verdicts.trueWording: Why not say 'tobacco', since the plant is 'a variety probably of Nicotiana'? Because the word would sound wrong
verdicts.note: Same raw book text, ch. 3 'The Bourgeois Burglar', around the p. 63-64 running heads. Quote 'a variety probably of Nicotiana' verbatim, and the pipe-weed-not-tobacco reason is verbatim ('Because the word would sound wrong ... It is an import from some unknown Caribbean language via Spanish'). The only defective limb is the botanical label: a binomial needs genus plus species, and neither Shippey nor the Prologue supplies one.
